Just for completeness.
I found why the visibility_timeout seemed to not be enforced.
I noticed that when I lowered the visibility_timeout, my tasks got re-added on the lower timeout.
When i increased the visibility_timeout the tasks kept being re-added after an hour.

Turns out one of my metrics scraper we use for Prometheus metrics instantiated a `Celery` object with the default config to get active worker information. This instance also started the event loop that calls `restore_visible` which was responsible for the behaviour i observed.

I now worked around it by setting 
`app.conf.broker_transport_options = "visibility_timeout": float("inf")}`
on the scraper so it does not interfere with others, now all works as expected.

I don't think this is a bug, yet.

Visibility timeout (for SQS and redis) and eta/countdown and acks_late (separate things but similar issue) is a known problem. Acks late isn't necessarily documented with this issue but I think it's actually the same problem. We should update the docs.

Some of the docs around celery worker/cluster health have considerations around "stuck" workers. So maybe the worker is replying to a heartbeat and other pidbox (control/inspect) commands, but potentially it's stuck in some other way. I can't pretend I've ever really seen this happen (I've seen celery/encoding bugs crash the task runner but the worker reports all is good), but that doesn't mean it can't.

So, I recommend we document the issue (should we agree it's not a "bug" but an implementation detail), and then decide if we can fix it within the library (as opposed to the application devs writing locking code/check/database state checking).

If you use `--pool=solo` it will always `ack` after finishing the long-running task. So for long-running tasks, when `ack` time exceeds the **1 hour** the default of `visibility_timeout`(in my tests, less than 1 hour does not take effect as you must set `visibility_timeout` more than **1 hour** ), the task will be redelivered again and again in a loop. More at [visibility_timeout](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/stable/getting-started/backends-and-brokers/redis.html#visibility-timeout).

There is one more caveat in `solo`, **No heartbeat** sent in `solo`(However, I do not know whether it also causes the long-running task redelivery).

There are **some ways** for me to avoid long tasks being executed multiple times,

1. Run the bellowing instead of `--pool=solo`

```sh
celery --app project:app worker --pool=prefork --concurrency=1
```

2. Increase the `visibility_timeout` in Python code (as I do some tests, `visibility_timeout` below `1h` will not take effect. I don't know it's a bug or not),

```py
app = Celery()
app.conf.broker_transport_options = {"visibility_timeout": 36000} #10h
```

3. Set [worker_deduplicate_successful_tasks](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/stable/userguide/configuration.html#worker-deduplicate-successful-tasks) to avoid re-running even after the worker receives the duplicate task again.

```py
app.conf.worker_deduplicate_successful_tasks = True
```

I encountered the same issue in Project A, where setting the visibility timeout to over 4 hours seemed ineffective; long-running tasks repeated every hour. However, when I set the visibility timeout to 1 minute, it seemed to take effect again. 

Eventually, I discovered that it might be because I had **multiple Python projects using Celery sharing the same Redis instance**.

 In the other projects, the visibility timeout was set to the default value, which could have caused **interference between different projects' visibility timeouts**. Smaller values would override larger ones. 

My solution was to allocate a **separate Redis instance for Project A,** and now everything is running smoothly. 



Additionally, I'm using Celery version 5.3.6, where setting the visibility timeout requires configuring three values: 


app.conf.broker_transport_options = {'visibility_timeout': 14400}
app.conf.result_backend_transport_options = {'visibility_timeout': 14400}
app.conf.visibility_timeout = 14400

The "again and again" loop liviaerxin describes has a precise condition, and it isn't limited to the solo pool. An `acks_late` task that runs longer than the visibility timeout reruns without end when its worker can't take a second message: one pool process with `worker_prefetch_multiplier=1`, or `worker_disable_prefetch`. With room for a second message it stops after a few runs. | One 5 s task, `visibility_timeout=2`, prefork `-c 1`, watched for 40 s | Runs | | --- | --- | | `worker_prefetch_multiplier=1` | 8, one every 5 s until the end | | `worker_disable_prefetch=True` | 8, the same | | `worker_prefetch_multiplier=2` | 3, then done | | Multiplier 1 with `worker_deduplicate_successful_tasks=True` and a result backend | 1, and the copy is skipped | | The same with a 1 s task | 1 | The restore sweep puts the message back while the first run is still going, and removes its record. A worker with no room fetches that copy only after the first run acks, so the ack doesn't find a record to remove. The copy gets a record of its own, runs past the timeout, and the same state comes back. A worker with room fetches the copy while the first run is still going. A restored message keeps its delivery tag, so the first run's ack removes the copy's record, and the reruns end. `acks_late` with a multiplier of 1 is what the optimizing guide recommends for long tasks, and the Redis caveat names the loop only for ETA, countdown and retry. Would a docs PR help that adds this case, and says that a visibility timeout above the longest task or `worker_deduplicate_successful_tasks` ends it?
Reproduction: tasks.py, run.py and output ```python # tasks.py import time import redis from celery import Celery app = Celery("tasks", broker="redis://localhost:6379/0") app.conf.task_acks_late = True # 2 s stands for the default hour; the sweep runs every second. app.conf.broker_transport_options = { "visibility_timeout": 2, "unacked_restore_interval": 1, "unacked_restore_throttle": 1, } log = redis.Redis(db=1) @app.task def long_task(): log.rpush("runs", time.time()) time.sleep(5) ``` ```python # run.py import time from tasks import log, long_task log.delete("runs") long_task.delay() time.sleep(40) starts = [float(t) for t in log.lrange("runs", 0, -1)] print(len(starts), "runs, started at", [round(t - starts[0]) for t in starts], "seconds") ``` ```console $ celery -A tasks worker -c 1 --prefetch-multiplier=1 --without-gossip --without-mingle --without-heartbeat $ python run.py 8 runs, started at [0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35] seconds $ celery -A tasks worker -c 1 --prefetch-multiplier=2 --without-gossip --without-mingle --without-heartbeat $ python run.py 3 runs, started at [0, 5, 10] seconds ``` Celery main (9c2f238), kombu main (445027e), Redis 7.4, Python 3.14. The run uses no fault injection. The short timeout only makes it fast. With the default of one hour, a task longer than an hour reruns the same way.
